lessons.title: Percentages
lessons.subject: Math
learning_objectives: Understand percentage as parts per hundred
Convert between percentages, decimals, fractions
Calculate percentages of amounts
lessons.reading_material:
Percent means 'per hundred'. 50% means 50 out of 100, or 1/2. 25% = 25/100 = 1/4. To find 30% of 80: 80 × 30 ÷ 100 = 24. Percentages are everywhere: discounts in shops, test scores, statistics. Key conversions: 1/2=50%, 1/4=25%, 3/4=75%, 1/5=20%, 1/10=10%.

Here's a simple way to think about why this lesson matters. Learning Math is a bit like building with blocks -- each new idea rests on the ideas that came before it. Percentages is one of the blocks near the bottom of this particular tower, which is exactly why it's worth taking the time to understand it properly now rather than rushing past it.

Here is what success looks like for this lesson: Understand percentage as parts per hundred; Convert between percentages, decimals, fractions; Calculate percentages of amounts. If you can honestly say you can do all of these by the time you finish, you've learned the lesson properly, not just skimmed it.

Some important terms appear in this lesson: percent, per hundred, percentage of amounts, conversion. Try this trick: after reading through the lesson once, cover the page and see if you can explain each of these words to yourself (or better, to someone else) without peeking. If you get stuck on one, that's exactly the word to go back and reread about.

A common mistake with lessons like this one is memorising a fact without understanding why it's true. Memorised facts fade quickly and don't help when a question is asked in a slightly different way. Understanding, on the other hand, sticks around and lets you handle questions you've never seen before -- so whenever you can, ask yourself 'why is that true?' rather than just 'what is the answer?'

Try this to reinforce what you just learned: VAT calculation role play; Sale discount problems. It only takes a few minutes, but actively doing something with the idea works much better for memory than simply rereading the lesson a second time.

For homework, Calculate: 15% of 60, 40% of 150, 75% of 200, 8% of 250. This isn't just busywork -- it's a chance to use today's lesson somewhere outside the lesson itself, which is exactly how you'll know whether you really understood it or only thought you did.

lessons.subject: Math

lessons.title: Climate Change
lessons.subject: Geography
learning_objectives: Explain the greenhouse effect
Describe the causes and effects of climate change
lessons.reading_material:
The greenhouse effect keeps Earth warm naturally. But burning fossil fuels releases excess CO₂, trapping more heat. This causes global warming: rising temperatures, melting ice caps, sea level rise, more extreme weather. Solutions: reduce emissions, renewable energy, reforestation.

Here's a simple way to think about why this lesson matters. Learning Geography is a bit like building with blocks -- each new idea rests on the ideas that came before it. Climate Change is one of the blocks near the bottom of this particular tower, which is exactly why it's worth taking the time to understand it properly now rather than rushing past it.

Here is what success looks like for this lesson: Explain the greenhouse effect; Describe the causes and effects of climate change. If you can honestly say you can do all of these by the time you finish, you've learned the lesson properly, not just skimmed it.

Some important terms appear in this lesson: greenhouse effect, global warming, CO₂, fossil fuels, sea level, emissions. Try this trick: after reading through the lesson once, cover the page and see if you can explain each of these words to yourself (or better, to someone else) without peeking. If you get stuck on one, that's exactly the word to go back and reread about.

A common mistake with lessons like this one is memorising a fact without understanding why it's true. Memorised facts fade quickly and don't help when a question is asked in a slightly different way. Understanding, on the other hand, sticks around and lets you handle questions you've never seen before -- so whenever you can, ask yourself 'why is that true?' rather than just 'what is the answer?'

Try this to reinforce what you just learned: Graph temperature data over 100 years; Debate: what can students do about climate change?. It only takes a few minutes, but actively doing something with the idea works much better for memory than simply rereading the lesson a second time.

For homework, Calculate your family's approximate carbon footprint for one week. This isn't just busywork -- it's a chance to use today's lesson somewhere outside the lesson itself, which is exactly how you'll know whether you really understood it or only thought you did.

When it's time to revise this topic before a test, remember: Review this lesson before the next class. A quick way to check yourself is to try explaining the whole lesson out loud in under a minute, as if you were teaching it to a younger student -- if you can do that smoothly, you're ready.

So, in short: Climate Change matters because it connects to bigger ideas coming later in Geography. Don't worry if it doesn't feel completely natural on the first read -- that's normal for any new idea. Read it again, try the practice activity, and check yourself against the learning goals above; understanding usually arrives on the second or third pass, not the first.

It's worth pausing to ask why Climate Change is part of the Geography curriculum at all. Every topic you study at school is chosen because it either explains something about the world you can see for yourself, or because it builds a mental tool you will keep using in more advanced lessons later. Climate Change is one of those building-block topics: once you understand it well, several things that used to feel confusing in Geography start to make a lot more sense.

Before getting into the details, think about where Climate Change shows up outside of the classroom. Ideas in Geography are rarely just for tests -- they usually connect to things you notice in everyday life, and part of getting good at Geography is training yourself to spot those connections instead of treating school topics as separate from the rest of the world.

lessons.title: World Poetry
lessons.subject: World Literature
learning_objectives: Identify poetic devices (simile, metaphor, imagery)
Analyse poems from different cultures
Write a short poem inspired by world poetry
lessons.reading_material:
Poetry exists in every culture and language. Pablo Neruda (Chile) wrote passionate love poems and political verse. Rabindranath Tagore (India) won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913 for 'Gitanjali'. Mahmoud Darwish (Palestine) expressed longing for homeland. Matsuo Bashō (Japan) perfected the haiku form (5-7-5 syllables). Emily Dickinson (USA) wrote quiet, powerful poems about death and nature. Poetic devices: simile (like/as), metaphor (direct comparison), imagery (sensory language), personification (giving human traits to objects).

Here's a simple way to think about why this lesson matters. Learning World Literature is a bit like building with blocks -- each new idea rests on the ideas that came before it. World Poetry is one of the blocks near the bottom of this particular tower, which is exactly why it's worth taking the time to understand it properly now rather than rushing past it.

Here is what success looks like for this lesson: Identify poetic devices (simile, metaphor, imagery); Analyse poems from different cultures; Write a short poem inspired by world poetry. If you can honestly say you can do all of these by the time you finish, you've learned the lesson properly, not just skimmed it.

Some important terms appear in this lesson: Simile, Metaphor, Imagery, Personification, Haiku, Nobel Prize. Try this trick: after reading through the lesson once, cover the page and see if you can explain each of these words to yourself (or better, to someone else) without peeking. If you get stuck on one, that's exactly the word to go back and reread about.

A common mistake with lessons like this one is memorising a fact without understanding why it's true. Memorised facts fade quickly and don't help when a question is asked in a slightly different way. Understanding, on the other hand, sticks around and lets you handle questions you've never seen before -- so whenever you can, ask yourself 'why is that true?' rather than just 'what is the answer?'

Try this to reinforce what you just learned: Write a haiku inspired by nature; read aloud a poem from a culture different from your own. It only takes a few minutes, but actively doing something with the idea works much better for memory than simply rereading the lesson a second time.

When it's time to revise this topic before a test, remember: Read poetry aloud — the sound reveals meaning. A quick way to check yourself is to try explaining the whole lesson out loud in under a minute, as if you were teaching it to a younger student -- if you can do that smoothly, you're ready.

lessons.title: Perspective and Composition
lessons.subject: Art
learning_objectives: Apply one-point perspective in drawings
Use the rule of thirds in composition
lessons.reading_material:
Perspective creates the illusion of depth. One-point perspective: parallel lines converge at a vanishing point. The rule of thirds: divide the page into 9 sections (3×3 grid) and place key subjects at the intersections — creates balanced, interesting compositions. Renaissance artists like Leonardo mastered perspective.

Know how to call for help near water

H.E.L.P. position (Heat Escape Lessening Posture): pull knees to chest to conserve body heat in cold water. info_cards.title: Did You Know?

info_cards.title: Famous Places
info_cards.fact: The Sydney Opera House in Australia has a roof made of more than a million small ceramic tiles.

info_cards.title: Philosophical Quote
info_cards.fact: "He who has a why to live can bear almost any how." — Friedrich Nietzsche, German philosopher.

info_cards.title: Famous Quote
info_cards.fact: "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind." — Neil Armstrong, astronaut.

info_cards.title: Famous Person: Nelson Mandela
info_cards.fact: Nelson Mandela spent 27 years in prison for opposing apartheid in South Africa and later became the country's first democratically elected president.

info_cards.title: Book Summary: Sapiens
info_cards.fact: "Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind" by Yuval Noah Harari (2011) traces the history of the human species from prehistoric foragers to the modern world.

info_cards.title: Book Summary: The Wright Brothers
info_cards.fact: "The Wright Brothers" by David McCullough tells the true story of how Orville and Wilbur Wright invented and flew the first successful airplane.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Stephen Hawking
info_cards.fact: "However difficult life may seem, there is always something you can do and succeed at." — British theoretical physicist known for his work on black holes and his book A Brief History of Time.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Carl Sagan
info_cards.fact: "Somewhere, something incredible is waiting to be known." — American astronomer and science communicator who hosted the television series Cosmos.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Richard Feynman
info_cards.fact: "I would rather have questions that can't be answered than answers that can't be questioned." — American theoretical physicist who won the Nobel Prize for his work on quantum electrodynamics.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Niels Bohr
info_cards.fact: "An expert is a person who has made all the mistakes that can be made in a very narrow field." — Danish physicist who made foundational contributions to understanding atomic structure and quantum theory.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Max Planck
info_cards.fact: "Science cannot solve the ultimate mystery of nature." — German physicist whose work founded quantum theory, for which he won the Nobel Prize.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Werner Heisenberg
info_cards.fact: "What we observe is not nature itself, but nature exposed to our method of questioning." — German physicist known for the uncertainty principle, a cornerstone of quantum mechanics.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Dmitri Mendeleev
info_cards.fact: "There is nothing in this world that I fear more than to have my words exceed my deeds." — Russian chemist who created the periodic table of elements, predicting the existence of undiscovered elements.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Michael Faraday
info_cards.fact: "Nothing is too wonderful to be true." — British scientist whose discoveries in electromagnetism led to the invention of the electric motor.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: James Clerk Maxwell
info_cards.fact: "The true logic of this world is in the calculus of probabilities." — Scottish physicist whose equations unified electricity, magnetism, and light into one theory of electromagnetism.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Gregor Mendel
info_cards.fact: "Nature... follows established laws... and the same laws must... be applicable to all variable organisms." — Austrian monk and scientist whose pea-plant experiments founded the science of genetics.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Louis Pasteur
info_cards.fact: "Chance favors the prepared mind." — French scientist who developed the process of pasteurization and helped establish the germ theory of disease.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Alexander Fleming
info_cards.fact: "One sometimes finds what one is not looking for." — Scottish scientist who discovered penicillin, the first widely used antibiotic.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Edward Jenner
info_cards.fact: "I should be ill indeed if I did not feel myself fully repaid by the enjoyment of the present." — English physician who developed the first vaccine, protecting against smallpox.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Ada Lovelace
info_cards.fact: "That brain of mine is something more than merely mortal; as time will show." — English mathematician regarded as the first computer programmer for her work on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Alan Turing
info_cards.fact: "Sometimes it is the people no one imagines anything of who do the things that no one can imagine." — British mathematician whose work laid the foundations of computer science and helped break Nazi codes in WWII.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Grace Hopper
info_cards.fact: "It's easier to ask forgiveness than it is to get permission." — American computer scientist and Navy admiral who helped develop one of the earliest programming languages, COBOL.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Tim Berners-Lee
info_cards.fact: "This is for everyone." — British computer scientist who invented the World Wide Web in 1989.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Steve Jobs
info_cards.fact: "Your time is limited, so don't waste it living someone else's life." — American entrepreneur who co-founded Apple Inc. and helped popularize personal computers and smartphones.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Bill Gates
info_cards.fact: "It's fine to celebrate success but it is more important to heed the lessons of failure." — American entrepreneur who co-founded Microsoft and later focused on global health and education philanthropy.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Hedy Lamarr
info_cards.fact: "Hope and curiosity about the future seemed better than guarantees." — Austrian-American actress and inventor whose frequency-hopping work helped lay groundwork for modern wireless technology.

lessons.title: World Leaders and History Makers
lessons.subject: General Knowledge
learning_objectives: Identify influential historical and modern figures
Explain their contributions
Discuss the importance of leadership
lessons.reading_material:
Throughout history, individuals have changed the world. Malala Yousafzai fought for girls' education. Nelson Mandela ended apartheid in South Africa. Marie Curie won two Nobel Prizes in science. Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) transformed the Arabian Peninsula with Islam. These figures inspire us through courage, perseverance, and service to others. Leadership means taking responsibility for others, not just having power.

Before getting into the details, think about where World Leaders and History Makers shows up outside of the classroom. Ideas in General Knowledge are rarely just for tests -- they usually connect to things you notice in everyday life, and part of getting good at General Knowledge is training yourself to spot those connections instead of treating school topics as separate from the rest of the world.

Here is what success looks like for this lesson: Identify influential historical and modern figures; Explain their contributions; Discuss the importance of leadership. If you can honestly say you can do all of these by the time you finish, you've learned the lesson properly, not just skimmed it.

Some important terms appear in this lesson: Leader, Influence, Nobel Prize, Activist, Historical Figure, Legacy. Try this trick: after reading through the lesson once, cover the page and see if you can explain each of these words to yourself (or better, to someone else) without peeking. If you get stuck on one, that's exactly the word to go back and reread about.

A common mistake with lessons like this one is memorising a fact without understanding why it's true. Memorised facts fade quickly and don't help when a question is asked in a slightly different way. Understanding, on the other hand, sticks around and lets you handle questions you've never seen before -- so whenever you can, ask yourself 'why is that true?' rather than just 'what is the answer?'

Try this to reinforce what you just learned: Class timeline: each student researches one figure and places them on a world history timeline. It only takes a few minutes, but actively doing something with the idea works much better for memory than simply rereading the lesson a second time.

When it's time to revise this topic before a test, remember: Think about local heroes too — impact does not have to be global. A quick way to check yourself is to try explaining the whole lesson out loud in under a minute, as if you were teaching it to a younger student -- if you can do that smoothly, you're ready.

So, in short: World Leaders and History Makers matters because it connects to bigger ideas coming later in General Knowledge. Don't worry if it doesn't feel completely natural on the first read -- that's normal for any new idea. Read it again, try the practice activity, and check yourself against the learning goals above; understanding usually arrives on the second or third pass, not the first.

World Leaders and History Makers is one of the blocks near the bottom of this particular tower, which is exactly why it's worth taking the time to understand it properly now rather than rushing past it.

One thing that trips learners up with topics like this is going too fast: skimming the words without picturing what they actually mean. If a sentence in this lesson feels confusing, try slowing down and picturing a real example in your head, or drawing a quick sketch -- turning words into a picture is one of the best ways to catch a misunderstanding before it becomes a habit.

lessons.title: Nutrition and Balanced Meals
lessons.subject: Cooking
learning_objectives: Identify the main food groups
Plan a balanced meal
Understand the role of nutrients
lessons.reading_material:
The five main food groups are: Carbohydrates (bread, rice, pasta — energy), Proteins (meat, fish, eggs, beans — growth and repair), Dairy (milk, cheese — calcium for bones), Fruits and Vegetables (vitamins and minerals), Fats and Sugars (energy in small amounts). A balanced meal includes foods from each group. The Eatwell Plate (UK) or MyPlate (USA) visually shows healthy proportions. Fibre (from vegetables and whole grains) aids digestion.

It's worth pausing to ask why Nutrition and Balanced Meals is part of the Cooking curriculum at all. Every topic you study at school is chosen because it either explains something about the world you can see for yourself, or because it builds a mental tool you will keep using in more advanced lessons later. Nutrition and Balanced Meals is one of those building-block topics: once you understand it well, several things that used to feel confusing in Cooking start to make a lot more sense.

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to do a few specific things: Identify the main food groups; Plan a balanced meal; Understand the role of nutrients. Keep these goals in mind as you read -- they're not just a checklist for the teacher, they're a way for you to test yourself afterwards and see whether the lesson has really sunk in.

The key words to know for this lesson are: Food Groups, Carbohydrates, Proteins, Dairy, Vitamins, Minerals. New topics often come with new vocabulary, and in Cooking the vocabulary usually isn't just decoration -- each of these words points to a specific idea that you'll need again in later lessons, so it's worth being able to explain each one in your own words, not just recognise it when you see it.

One thing that trips learners up with topics like this is going too fast: skimming the words without picturing what they actually mean. If a sentence in this lesson feels confusing, try slowing down and picturing a real example in your head, or drawing a quick sketch -- turning words into a picture is one of the best ways to catch a misunderstanding before it becomes a habit.

A good way to practise this lesson is: Design a healthy weekly meal plan covering all 5 food groups. Doing something hands-on with an idea -- rather than only reading about it -- is one of the fastest ways to make it stick, because your brain remembers things you've actually done far better than things you've only read.

When it's time to revise this topic before a test, remember: Half your plate should be fruit and vegetables. A quick way to check yourself is to try explaining the whole lesson out loud in under a minute, as if you were teaching it to a younger student -- if you can do that smoothly, you're ready.

To wrap up: Nutrition and Balanced Meals is one small piece of Cooking, but it's a piece worth knowing solidly, because later lessons will lean on it without stopping to re-explain it. Take your time with it now, ask questions if anything feels unclear, and come back to reread this lesson whenever a later topic reminds you of it -- that kind of revisiting is exactly how real understanding builds up over a school year.

lessons.reading_material:

For example, Saudi Arabia exports oil; Bangladesh exports textiles; Japan exports technology. This interdependence means countries rely on each other.
